title: Merge Intervals
description:
# Merge Intervals

You are given an array of closed intervals `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [starti, endi]` represents every point from `starti` through `endi`.

Merge every pair of intervals that overlaps and return a sorted array of non-overlapping intervals that covers exactly the same points as the input.

Two intervals overlap when they share at least one point. For example, `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` overlap because they both contain `4`, so they merge into `[1,5]`. The input intervals are not guaranteed to be sorted.

## Example 1:

**Input:** intervals = [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
**Output:** [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
**Explanation:** `[1,3]` and `[2,6]` overlap and merge into `[1,6]`. The other intervals stay separate.

## Example 2:

**Input:** intervals = [[1,4],[4,5]]
**Output:** [[1,5]]
**Explanation:** Closed intervals sharing endpoint `4` are considered overlapping.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= intervals.length <= 10^4`
*   `intervals[i].length == 2`
*   `0 <= starti <= endi <= 10^4`

solutions.name: Sort By Start And Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort intervals by start coordinate. Keep the last merged interval as the only interval that can still overlap the next sorted interval. If the next start is greater than the last merged end, append a new interval; otherwise extend the last end.

## Key Insight

After sorting by start, all intervals that belong to one merged component appear consecutively. Once a later interval starts after the current end, no earlier interval can connect it back.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), dominated by sorting.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the returned list stores the merged intervals.

solutions.name: Priority Queue Ordered Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert every interval into a priority queue ordered by start coordinate. Poll intervals in order and merge each one into the current output tail, exactly as if the intervals had been sorted first.

## Key Insight

The core requirement is processing intervals by nondecreasing start. A heap gives the same order without mutating the original array, which is useful when intervals arrive from a stream or another producer.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), because each interval is pushed and popped from the heap.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the heap and output list store intervals.

solutions.name: Separate Starts And Ends Sweep
solutions.description:
## Approach

Copy all starts into one array and all ends into another, then sort both arrays. A merged interval closes at `ends[i]` exactly when the next start is greater than that end. The next component starts at the next unused start.

## Key Insight

This separates interval merging into boundary events. For closed intervals, `starts[i + 1] == ends[i]` still means overlap, so the closing condition must be strictly `starts[i + 1] > ends[i]`.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), because the two boundary arrays are sorted.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because start and end arrays are stored.

solutions.name: Endpoint Event Sweep
solutions.description:
## Approach

Convert every interval into a start event and an end event stored by coordinate. Sweep coordinates in sorted order, processing starts before ends at the same coordinate. Open a merged interval when active coverage rises from zero and close it when coverage returns to zero.

## Key Insight

Start-before-end ordering is what makes closed endpoints merge correctly: `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` have active coverage through coordinate `4`, so they become one interval.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), because endpoint events are stored in a sorted map.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because each interval contributes boundary events.

solutions.name: Overlap Graph Components
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat each interval as a graph node. Two nodes are connected when their intervals overlap. Run DFS over this implicit graph; each connected component merges into one interval spanning the minimum start and maximum end among its nodes.

## Key Insight

Merging is transitive. If `A` overlaps `B` and `B` overlaps `C`, all three must share one output interval even when `A` and `C` do not directly overlap. The graph model makes that transitive closure explicit.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2), because each visited interval may compare against every other interval.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because visited flags, the DFS stack, and the output are linear.
